newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists say EMU entry political,no dogma.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists say EMU entry political,no dogma.

text.p: France's opposition Socialist party said on Wednesday it supported European monetary union but that moving to a single currency was a political decison and should not be clouded by dogmatic economic fitness criteria.

Spelling out policy as France's snap parliamentary election campaign got underway, Socialist economic policymaker Dominique Strauss-Kahn also said boosting purchasing power was the only way to stimulate the economy.
"We want the single currency. What we want is an instrument that allows us counterbalance American domination and help growth and employment," Strauss-Kahn told Le Monde newspaper.

"As far as the (monetary union) criteria are concerned, neither Germany nor France, to mention but two, will respect them all. A political decision will therefore apply, I hope," he said in an interview in the afternoon daily.

He made it clear, however, that the Socialist party was not saying the public deficit -- which has to be limited to three percent of economic output, or gross domestic product (GDP), to qualify for the euro -- should not be controlled.
"Even if it's clear public deficits cannot be allowed to slip, there is no point making an unjustified dogma out of the three percent (deficit limit) criterion," he said.

Purchasing power should be boosted to help stimulate growth of the economy, since it was not possible to help growth through interest rate policy and it was hard to see ways of doing so through budgetary measures.

"Economic stimulation through monetary policy is barred, budgetary stimulation is hard to see, what's left is stimulation through a boost in purchasing power," Strauss-Kahn, co-author of Socialist party economic policy, told the afternoon daily.

The Socialists have attacked the centre-right government's economic record on the grounds that spending cuts and austerity have hurt demand and growth prospects as the country fights to cut its public deficit in 1997 to qualify for monetary union.
Strauss-Kahn said a reduction in work-time without a loss in salary would help to stimulate the economy and that creating jobs for young people would strengthen the demand needed to support growth.

France's parliamentary poll, which Conservative President Jacques Chirac has brought forward by ten months to try to secure a fresh mandate for reform of the economy and the state, takes place in two rounds on May 25 and June 1.
